<reason>Side A built a more compelling causal narrative linking youth engagement to future institutional survival, effectively reframing "universal service" to include underserved youth rather than just legacy demographics. A's decisive distinction that "encounter is a precondition for education" neutralized B's depth argument, while A's budget comparison (short-form extending existing reporting versus channel expansion's fixed transmission costs) undercut B's cannibalization claim. Though A's Rebuttal 2 was clipped for exceeding word limits, the visible portion answered pressure questions sharply. B made strong institutional arguments about depth and universal access but struggled to explain how channel expansion creates the youth familiarity necessary for B's own "trust when the feed fails" thesis.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Pressure Questions (Turn 5) exposed a circularity in Side B's position: B claimed broadcasters must be trusted "when the feed fails," but A forced B to explain how expanding linear channels—formats youth do not watch—creates that familiarity, and why transmission spending is less cannibalistic than short-form production.</best_rebuttal>
